Neoplatonism. A philosophical school that reinterpreted Plato through a mystical, hierarchical lens, emerging in the third century CE and dominating late ancient thought until the closure of philosophical schools in the sixth century. It posits a hierarchy of reality descending from the One—ultimate reality—through intelligence and soul to matter, with the goal of achieving mystical union with the divine. Its synthesis of reason and mysticism profoundly influenced Christian theology, Islamic philosophy, and Renaissance art.

Plotinus founded Neoplatonism, living from two hundred four to two hundred seventy CE. He systematized Platonism into a coherent metaphysical system centered on emanation—the flow of reality from the One. The One is utterly transcendent, ineffable, beyond being, knowledge, and description; all reality emanates from it.

The hierarchy of emanation descends like this: the One flows into Intellect—divine mind—which flows into Soul, comprising both world-soul and individual souls—which flows into Matter, the inert, lowest principle.

Mysticism is integral to Neoplatonism. Through philosophy, purification, and contemplation, the soul can achieve henosis, mystical union with the One. Plotinus taught in Rome, and his followers compiled his writings into the Enneads, fifty-four treatises that became the foundational texts of Neoplatonism.

The principle of emanation differs from creation. Reality flows from the One necessarily and eternally, not through will or choice. Porphyry, Plotinus's student, systematized Neoplatonic doctrines and added a crucial modification: souls have individual responsibilities and levels of spiritual development.

Neoplatonism heavily influenced medieval and Renaissance thought through Christian, Islamic, and Jewish philosophers who integrated Neoplatonic ideas into monotheistic theology. Michelangelo drew on Neoplatonic aesthetics: the fusion of divine and human beauty, the soul's ascent through sensory to intellectual beauty.

Neoplatonism is distinct from Stoicism but shares the emphasis on a unified, ordered cosmos and the soul's return to cosmic principles.

Neoplatonism connects to Plato, the ancient philosopher whose ideas it reinterprets and systematizes. The One is the transcendent source of all reality in Neoplatonic metaphysics. Stoicism shares emphasis on cosmic order and the integration of individual soul into universal principles. Christianity was deeply influenced through thinkers like Augustine and Pseudo-Dionysius. Michelangelo and the Renaissance periods integrated Neoplatonic texts and ideals. Being is central to Neoplatonic metaphysics in its hierarchy descending from the One.
